content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes a method to find a threshold for outlier detection which is then to be applied. 
The paper starts with an observation that normal data has often two sets of samples, one with fairly low outlier scores and one with rather high scores.

The authors propose to fit a polynomial to the sorted normal scores, then to take the maximum value of the fitted polynomial over the normal data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
It addresses an aspect which is often ignored - how to determine the threshold.
Experiments are done with outliers being classes from the same dataset as well as from other datasets. 

Weaknesses: 
Proposed method has a number of technical issues.

minor: 1. Eq (3) and (8) seems to be incorrect as formula and is not what the authors actually used.
The maximum of a polynomial is +inf if the leading coefficient is positive. 

What the authors did was to take the maximum of the fit values on the normal dataset - see figure 5.

minor:  2. Eq(6) has two issues. Firstly, optimizing degree using it does not depend on the cardinalities of \mathcal{N} and \mathcal{A}. They are unnecessary added complexities. 
Secondly, it has nothing to do with accuracy. The usage of accuracy there is misleading.
 Compactness is undefined what it should be.

minor:  3. Fitting a polynomial to the large flat low scoring part is not meaningful when one is interested only in the largest values.

major: 4. If the authors just take the highest polynomial fit value, then this method is questionable. The result for proper fitting with degree of at least 3 should be very close to the maximum of the sorted scores which were used to fit it. 

But then one can simply take the maximum over the raw scores , or  threshold along quantile scores for high values (or take the maximum as extreme value), which does the same in a simpler way. 

major: 5. Figure 5 and figure 4 suggests that the results were tuned by early stopping of the polynomial fitting optimization. 

This is because after convergence in figure 5 it returns simply the maximum of the scores of the normal dataset, which can be achieved without any polynomial fitting.
This is also supported by figure 4, where a simple linear normalization improves the fitting outcome. With proper optimization this should not occur and one should obtain the same fit.

But if that is the essential gain using this method, then , firstly, it uses a hidden parameter in an non-transparent way to achieve good scores (the amount of optimization steps), and secondly, one could achieve this much simpler by thresholding along high quantile values (this also would use sorting but skips fitting a parametric model). 

major: 6. Using the max of fitted scores does not make use of the L-trend described in section 4, thus the title is misleading. Reason is that the maximum merely looks at the very top of the normal data, if the polynomial is fitted well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper reads ok.

Novelty: if the results hold, it would be somewhat novel indeed.

About reproducibility:
A base code is provided but not the full set of experiments.

The results are unexpectedly bad for the default threshold selection of the baseline methods.
Shell and OC seem to select very low thresholds resulting in high recall and low precision.
The results for DRAE in F1 on other datasets are not comparable but they are not as low as in this paper on the dataset used here.

How these thresholds have been selected for the baseline methods?

Quality: There are more than minor concerns about weaknesses and reproducibility stated above.

Some unclear or misleading parts:

1. Most previous anomaly detectors tend to explore the normality. Drawn a lesson from the above
analysis, we suggest the anomalous pattern also should be considered. We believe that anomalies are
not only different from normal instances but also vary from other anomalous data. 

the paper uses only the normal data.

2. Table 6 writes for MNIST raw pixels, but Section 6 says that resnet features are extracted. What is actually done ?

Minor comment: 
The F1 score is also sensitive to the contamination rate: https://2021.ecmlpkdd.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/sub_406.pdf . This makes comparisons difficult unless the contamination rate is kept constant.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an adaptive thresholding method for anomaly detection.
As stated in the paper, the majority of anomaly detection papers focus on estimating anomaly scores but how to find a threshold is underexplored. The paper directly tackles this overlooked but important topic in anomaly detection studies. The idea is to fit a polynomial curve to the distribution of normal samples and detect anomalies that do not fit the curve. Experiments on five in-distribution scenarios and two out-of-distribution scenarios validate the strong performance of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

### Extensive experiments with different baseline methods.
The paper performed experiments on five in-distribution scenarios and two out-of-distribution scenarios which sufficiently shows the effectiveness of the method. In addition, the base methods used to estimate anomaly scores are diverse and recent ones, including OCSVM variants, and autoencoder based methods. The performance gain is significant over the other thresholding methods in most cases.

### Comparison with the oracle performance is shown (F1-ratio)
The paper reports the upper bound performance when the optimal threshold is used.
This is an important analysis and is addressed in the paper.




## Weakness

### Important experiment details are missing

The paper does not describe the anomaly ratio used for the experiments, training epochs, optimizer, learning rates, and other details about model training.
Moreover, the provided code barely includes any information for reproducibility.
This makes me have a serious concern about the reproducibility of the paper.

### Several clarification issues and minor mistakes in writing.

The paper has to correct minor errors and clarify terms that are used without clear definitions.
Refer to the Clarity section.

### A claim without supported experiments.

Figure5 demonstrates that the proposed method can be used to clean the normal dataset.
However, there is no experiment that supports the effectiveness of this application.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

- On page2 of the Introduction section, the sentence says anomaly ratios are often low. 
‘In many cases, thresholds are so badly estimated that Precision or Recall is almost zero. As the anomaly ratio is usually less than 0.01’
Does the paper perform experiments on such a low anomaly ratio? What are anomaly ratios used in the experiments?

- It is hard to understand the following sentence on page 2.
‘It is troublesome that cover the given score function Z(°§) into mathematics.’

- On page 2, the following part describes the density of anomalies and normal samples, but equations show the cardinality of anomalies and normal samples. ‘much lower density: |A| ≪ |N |.’

- [Question] When calculating var(Z(A)) or var(Z(N)), the variation already normalizes its scale by the number of samples. In equations (4) and (5), why do we have to normalize by the number of samples (|A| or |N|) again?

- The term ‘normalization’ or ‘true normalization’ in the caption of Figure 4 is not used nor defined in the remaining texts. What does normalization exactly mean?


### Quality

The writing has to be improved including clarification issues.
The experiments are extensive and sufficient, and the results are significant.

### Novelty

Although technically simple, the paper tackles an underexplored but important topic.

### Reproducibility

The paper has an issue with reproducibility.
Readers may not be able to reproduce the experiments with the current version of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper tackles an important and overlooked problem in anomaly detection.
Experiments are extensive and results are significant.
However, the paper has to be polished and clarify the missing details.
Most importantly, the reproducibility issue should be addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes threshold learning for unsupervised visual anomaly detection. This approach is accompanied with a novel "L-TREND PRIOR” and its optimization algorithms. The experiments verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

(1) The paper is well-organized and the presentation is generally clear.

(2) The motivation of “L-trend” is clear. The method is intuitive but reasonable.

Weaknesses：

(1) I generally agree with the authors with respect to the observation and intuition, although I don't think threshold learning is as important as score generating for visual anomaly detection. However, the main weakness is the applicability of the method, especially the learning-based curve fitting. The practicality of claims has not been demonstrated in some conditions and has subjective problems. E.g.,

- Section 1: The trade-off still exists even the proposed method define a threshold (how to discriminate anomaly from near-OOD samples?).

- Section 1: It seems that threshold learning may fail on the assumption “anomalies only slightly more different from the normal instance, than normal instances are from each other” in many cases. Because if we have contaminated scores, we cannot use a well-estimated threshold to distinguish them.

- Section 1: The claim “an anomalous instance is not only different from normal observations but varies from other anomalies” is correct, but why “threshold learning can be quite easy”? If anomalous instance varies from other anomalies, they may yield high anomaly score of the same distribution rather than different high anomaly scores. 

- Section 2: It is claimed in related work that normal samples are not available in most cases, but is this a general assumption?
Section 5.1: The motivation and practical role of curve fitting are questionable, especially the $max$ operation and the choice of $d_{max}$ which are closely related to the shape of "L-trend" (distribution of the generated score), but there is no experimental or theoretical proof that this distribution could always hold. 

- Eq 6 and Eq 7: if there are few instances in anomaly set, the variance estimation will be inaccurate, eventually affecting the selection of threshold. With the increase of the number of anomalies (such as simply copy the anomalies), the increase in the tail of "L trend" slows down, which makes it easier to fit the abnormal samples. At the same time, the "max" operation and "normalization" operation may further aggravate this problem.

- Since the authors claim that the proposed method can eliminate OOD-like normal samples, I hope they can explain whether the method has practical meaning by additional experiments, for example, whether using these "clean data" to retrain the unsupervised OOD detector is beneficial to obtain better anomaly detection performance.

(2) Sine minor points:

- The concepts between “anomaly detection” and “OOD Detection” are different but not clearly presented.

- Figure 1: the word ”ID-Anomaly” is confusing without clear explanation. Do you mean “In-Distribution” or “In-Domain”?
The importance and theoretical essence of threshold learning should be further analyzed.

- Section 6.1: as for the MNIST dataset, why “rasterized pixels as image feature” is appropriate? Reminder that the appearances could have influence on original score distribution.

- Section 6.5: Ablation experiments or theoretical analysis should include more details, such as the mixing ratio, as this seems to have great impact on the “L-Trend”.

- The ablation study is not very helpful for understanding the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The overall organization and presentation are clear.

The proposed method is intuitive and novel, but has limitations as explained above.

I think the proposed method reproducible, though some implementation details are missing.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes an intuitive and novel method for visual anomaly detection. There are some key weaknesses with respect to the methodology, explanation and empirical study, thus I think it is a borderline work below the acceptance threshold.

content.title: Unsupervised Threshold Learning with "$L$"-trend Prior For Visual Anomaly Detection
content.abstract: This paper considers unsupervised threshold learning, a practical yet under-researched module of anomaly detection (AD) for image data. AD comprises two separate modules: score generation and threshold learning. Most existing studies are more curious about the first part. It is often assumed that if the scoring module is good, estimating an accurate threshold is within easy reach. However, we argue that in the context of computer vision, some challenges in high-dimensional space lead threshold estimation be a non-trivial problem. In this paper, we leverage the inherent difference between normal instances and anomalies by ranking their anomaly score, which shows a phenomenon that involves two distinct trends. We term it as the "$L$"-trend prior. With that finding, we utilize an adaptive polynomial regression model to determine the threshold. Unlike the classic threshold learners which rely on enough training samples or statistical assumptions, this method is plug-and-play that can be implemented into different anomaly score function among various datasets. Also, the evaluation results demonstrate an obvious improvement.
